payload.title: Reading the Rings
paragraphs: A core of wood no wider than a pencil can be drilled from a living pine without harming it. Under a lens the sample shows a row of pale and dark bands, one pair for every year the tree has lived. Wide bands mark seasons of rain and warmth; narrow ones record drought, cold, or the shadow of a taller neighbour. Because trees of the same species in the same valley answer the weather in the same way, their patterns can be matched like fingerprints.

By overlapping samples — a living tree with a beam from a farmhouse, that beam with a plank from an older church — researchers have built continuous records reaching back thousands of years in parts of Europe. The method fixes the year in which a piece of timber was cut, something radiocarbon dating cannot do. Museums now use it to check the age of panel paintings, and archaeologists to settle arguments about when a village was abandoned.

The limits are real. Tropical trees, which grow all year round, often produce no clear rings at all, and a single core taken from an unusual specimen can mislead. Specialists therefore insist on dozens of samples before they announce a date. Even so, the timber in an ordinary roof holds a record of summers that no written document ever mentioned.

payload.title: Switching Off the Sky
paragraphs: Ten years ago the streets of several small towns in northern Spain went noticeably darker. Old lamps that threw light in every direction were replaced with hooded ones that point only at the pavement, and the colour was changed from blue-white to a warm amber. Residents were told to expect complaints; what arrived instead were photographs of the Milky Way taken from bedroom windows.

The change was not made for astronomers alone. Insects are drawn to short blue wavelengths and die in their thousands around bright lamps, and the birds that feed on them follow. Doctors add that light leaking through curtains delays the body's own clock, which is why hotel rooms in these towns now feel darker than guests are used to. Councils, meanwhile, noticed something simpler: pointing light downwards meant fewer lamps were needed, and the electricity bill fell by roughly a third.

Not everyone was convinced at first. Some shopkeepers argued that dim streets would feel unsafe, and a few still do. Yet police figures in the towns have not moved in either direction, and surveys suggest that what people actually dislike is glare — a single fierce lamp that leaves everything beyond it in shadow. Softer light, aimed low, turns out to be easier to walk through than bright light aimed everywhere.
